Storyline 3: Appeals are rare, outcomes vary widely by agency, and DHS increasingly dominates¶

Storyline 1 looks at how requests are closed. This one asks: what happens after a requester appeals? How many appeal, and does the agency's initial decision change?

Early exploration summarized this stage as "about one third reversed or remanded". That summary needs unpacking: what the denominator includes, how much agencies differ, and what role DHS plays.

The finding in one sentence (Section 7): few requesters appeal (fewer than 2 per 100 requests processed); what happens on appeal depends mainly on the agency: outside DHS about one quarter of closed appeals are reversed or remanded, ranging across agencies from single digits to about 60%; and DHS increasingly dominates the appeal stage: in FY2025 it received 3.4 times as many appeals as two years earlier, appeals pending at year end rose about tenfold, and most of the added closures were closed for other reasons, without a decision on the merits.

Roadmap:

Section Question Finding
1 How many requesters appeal? 1.29–1.99 appeals per 100 requests processed; the FY2025 jump is almost all DHS
2 What happens on appeal? About one quarter reversed or remanded outside DHS; much higher at DHS; FY2008 is a special case
3 The denominator matters Among appeals decided on the merits, about one third outside DHS; DHS did not become stricter
4 How much do agencies differ? From single digits to about 60%; DOJ pulls the outside-DHS average down; inside DHS, CBP has replaced USCIS as the largest
5 What happened at DHS in FY2024–25? Appeals 3.4 times their FY2023 level, pending appeals surged, and most added closures had no decision on the merits (one or two years of data)
6 Does any single unit drive the findings? The main figures do not; DHS's high share comes largely from USCIS
7 The resulting story One sentence, key points, what not to say, leads, methods

Terms:

  • Appeal outcomes (Table 08; handbook Section VI.B) are affirmed; partly affirmed and partly reversed or remanded; completely reversed or remanded; and closed for other reasons (neither affirmed nor reversed, for example because the request is in litigation, the appeal is a duplicate, or it was premature). Reversed or remanded combines the two reversal categories and includes remands for further processing; it does not mean the requester received records.
  • Two denominators: all closed appeals ("of those who appealed, how many saw a change"), and appeals decided on the merits, i.e. affirmed + partly reversed + completely reversed ("of the appeals the agency actually reviewed, how many were changed").
  • Table 10 (handbook Section VI.C.(2)) lists the non-exemption reasons cited on appeal. Several may be cited per appeal, and they may be cited for affirmed or partly reversed appeals too, so Table 10 is not a breakdown of other closures. Table 11 gives the text behind Table 10's "other" reasons.
  • Abbreviations: DHS (Homeland Security) and its USCIS (Citizenship and Immigration Services), CBP (Customs and Border Protection), ICE (Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and PRIV (Privacy Office); DOJ (Justice) and its OIP (Office of Information Policy); SSA (Social Security Administration); SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission); EEOC (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission); FRB (Federal Reserve Board); DOL (Labor); DOS (State).

1. How many requesters appeal?¶

Appeals received in the year (Table 07) ÷ requests processed in the year (Table 01), expressed per 100 requests processed. This compares annual volumes; an appeal may concern a request from an earlier year, so it is not a per-request probability. Requests released in full seldom give reason to appeal (a requester may still appeal, for example, the adequacy of the search or fees), so a second denominator is shown: per 100 dispositions other than full release.

Section 1:

  • Appeals are rare: 1.29–1.99 appeals per 100 requests processed government-wide (the same to two decimals with the 12 Table 02 categories as the denominator). Per 100 dispositions other than full release: 1.53–2.93 government-wide, 1.12–2.25 at DHS and 2.07–3.96 outside DHS. All are single digits.
  • Outside DHS the rate fell: 1.92–2.37 per 100 processed in FY2012–22, then 1.55, 1.58 and 1.78 in FY2023–25. Part of this is a larger denominator (dispositions at VBA and EOIR jumped from FY2023; see Storyline 1), not necessarily less willingness to appeal.
  • The FY2025 government-wide jump is almost all DHS: government-wide from 1.34 to 1.96; DHS from 1.18 to 2.08, outside DHS only from 1.58 to 1.78 (Section 5).

2. What happens on appeal?¶

Table 08 "completely reversed or remanded" plus "partly affirmed, partly reversed or remanded", divided by all closed appeals, for all government, DHS and outside DHS, together with DHS's share of closed appeals.

Section 2:

  • Government-wide, the reversed-or-remanded share ranges from 22.7% to 44.8% in FY2008–25; "about one third" is only a rough summary.
  • Outside DHS, about one quarter: 20.6%–27.3% each year.
  • DHS is much higher: 48.2%–75.7% each year in FY2009–23, falling to 39.0% and 36.7% in FY2024–25 (Section 3). DHS's share of closed appeals rose from 25.3% in FY2008 to 55.0% in FY2025, so the government-wide figure increasingly reflects DHS.
  • FY2008 is a special case: DHS's 26.6% that year reflects a large number of closures for other reasons (Section 3), so DHS's range is stated from FY2009.
  • Some agencies are missing in FY2008–09: 26 agencies have no FY2008 data; in FY2010 they account for 6.5% of government closed appeals and 10.6% outside DHS, with a reversed-or-remanded share of 33.5%, above the other agencies outside DHS (24.8%). The outside-DHS values for FY2008–09 (21.4% and 24.4%) are therefore somewhat low.

3. The denominator matters¶

Table 08's four outcomes add up to 100%. First, stacked bars of the four outcomes each year, to see which outcome grew as DHS's reversal share fell; then a denominator of appeals decided on the merits; finally complete and partial reversals separately.

Section 3:

  • DHS's recent fall reflects a change in the mix of closures: DHS's other closures rose from 17.8% in FY2023 to 36.9% in FY2024 and 43.3% in FY2025, while affirmances also fell, from 33.8% to 24.1% and 20.0%. Both reversals and affirmances fell; other closures grew.
  • Among appeals decided on the merits, DHS did not fall: 58.8%, 61.8% and 64.8% in FY2023–25. This cannot be read as stricter review at DHS.
  • Two denominators, two statements: outside DHS, about one quarter of all closed appeals (20.6%–27.3%), and about one third of appeals decided on the merits (28.4%–39.5% in FY2009–25); also without DOJ, 34.6%–46.5% (Section 4). Both are given, each with the question it answers.
  • Complete and partial reversals moved in opposite directions at DHS: partial reversals fell from 59.4% in FY2010 and 27.9% in FY2021 to 4.1% in FY2025, while complete reversals rose from 16.3% and 26.3% to 32.7%. Outside DHS both are flat (complete 12.3%–17.7%, partial 7.8%–13.3%). Government-wide complete reversals rose from 13.4% to 25.7%, which should not be quoted alone as "reversals doubled".
  • The FY2008 special case is USCIS: DHS closed 2,590 appeals that year, 1,570 of them for other reasons, 1,425 at USCIS. USCIS cites "other" 1,177 times in Table 10, and Table 11 gives "failure to comply – attorney barred from immigration practice" (891) and "failure to comply – interim interest project" (286), both procedural reasons.

4. How much do agencies differ?¶

"About one quarter" is an average. The table and chart show agencies with at least 250 closed appeals in FY2021–25 combined, ordered by volume (not ranked); then DOJ's weight and the components inside DHS.

Section 4:

  • The differences are large: across the 22 agencies, the reversed-or-remanded share ranges from 2.8% (FRB) to 59.4% (SSA), median 24.1%. Other closures range from 6.3% (SEC) to 68.8% (DOL) of the denominator, so the agencies' shares are not directly comparable and are not ranked.
  • DOJ pulls the outside-DHS average down: DOJ accounts for 24.5%–48.0% of closed appeals outside DHS each year, with a reversed-or-remanded share of only 10.9%–20.7%. Outside DHS and also without DOJ, the share is 25.0%–32.9% each year, close to three in ten.
  • Inside DHS the largest unit changed: USCIS's share of DHS closed appeals fell from 83% in FY2008 to 25% in FY2025, while CBP's rose from 8% to 58%. The high shares come mainly from these two: USCIS 84% in FY2010 (when it closed 3,924 appeals, producing the 44.8% government-wide peak; that year DHS received 2,740 appeals but closed 5,325, cutting appeals pending at year end from 2,995 in FY2009 to 740, so DHS's 75.7%, its FY2009–23 high, came in a year of clearing a backlog of appeals) and 37% in FY2025; CBP 66% in FY2010 and 43% in FY2025. PRIV stays low (14%, 12% and 15% in FY2020, FY2023 and FY2025) and closed 1,488 appeals in FY2025, pulling the DHS average down.

5. DHS in FY2024–25: appeals more than tripled, more closures without a decision on the merits¶

This is the newest and largest change in the storyline, but it rests on one or two years of data, and FY2025 has no following-year report to check against, so it is presented as facts and leads, clearly labeled.

Section 5:

  • Volume: government-wide appeals received were 7,922–15,599 each year in FY2008–23 and 32,062 in FY2025, 17,619 more than in FY2023 (14,443), of which DHS accounts for 14,614. DHS received 6,050 appeals in FY2023, 10,557 in FY2024 and 20,664 in FY2025, 64.5% of the government total. USCIS went from 2,656 in FY2022 to 10,129 in FY2025, CBP from 3,687 to 8,409.
  • Not keeping up: DHS closed 12,707 appeals in FY2025, and its appeals pending at year end rose from 2,482 in FY2024 to 10,567. Government-wide appeal backlog (Table 26) was 3,011–5,955 in FY2008–24 and 11,654 in FY2025; of the 6,272 added in one year, 5,489 are at DHS.
  • Most added closures had no decision on the merits (Table 08): DHS closed 6,583 more appeals in FY2025 than in FY2023; 4,412 of them (67%) were closures for other reasons, against 464 more affirmances and 1,707 more reversals or remands. Other closures rose from 1,090 to 5,502, mainly at CBP (625 to 3,847).
  • Reasons DHS cites (Tables 10 and 11; a parallel fact, not a breakdown of the above): The reasons DHS cites most in Table 10 are "improper request" (2,253 in FY2025, 1,482 of them at CBP) and "other" (2,120, 2,062 of them at CBP); DHS also cites "records not reasonably described" 742 times in FY2024 and "not agency record" 477 times in FY2025. CBP's Table 11 text for "other" in FY2025 is "no component response to adjudicate" (1,155), "untimely" (824) and "moot" (83); in FY2024 it also includes "improper appeal" (1,003).
  • On the measures: Table 10 reasons may be cited several times per appeal and for affirmed appeals too, so they show which reasons DHS cites, not what other closures consist of. DHS's Table 10 totals for FY2023–25 (1,090, 3,416 and 5,519) are close to its Table 08 other closures (1,090, 3,376 and 5,502), but that is only a reference. Table 11 is free text merged only by letter case, so its counts are lower bounds.
  • What can be said: most of the added closures did not reach a review on the merits. What cannot: that DHS changed its classification, or became stricter.

6. Does any single unit drive the findings?¶

Each agency or component is removed in turn from all years (agencies without components count once), and the range of the three main figures is reported; then DHS's share is recalculated without USCIS or without CBP.

Section 6:

  • Appeals per 100 requests processed: at most 2.37 across 594 removals (removing all of DHS, i.e. outside DHS in FY2015).
  • Reversed or remanded / closed appeals outside DHS: between 19.0% (removing DOS) and 32.9% (removing DOJ's OIP) across 572 removals; 19.7%–32.9% from FY2009. "About one quarter" therefore carries a margin of roughly seven to eight points either way.
  • Reversed or remanded / appeals decided on the merits outside DHS: 26.9%–46.5%.
  • DHS's high share comes largely from USCIS: without USCIS, DHS is 34.4%–56.8% in FY2009–23 (48.2%–75.7% with it), still above outside DHS; without CBP, 42.4%–77.5%. In FY2024–25 it is 38.8% and 36.8% without USCIS, and 32.8% and 28.4% without CBP.

7. The resulting story¶

In one sentence: few requesters appeal; what happens on appeal depends mainly on the agency; and DHS increasingly dominates the appeal stage: in FY2025 it received 3.4 times as many appeals as two years earlier, appeals pending at year end rose about tenfold, and most of the added closures were closed for other reasons, without a decision on the merits.

Key points:

  1. Appeals are rare (Section 1): 1.29–1.99 appeals per 100 requests processed; 1.53–2.93 per 100 dispositions other than full release.
  2. Outside DHS, about one quarter are reversed or remanded (Sections 2 and 6): 20.6%–27.3% each year, 19.0%–32.9% after removing any single unit; about one third among appeals decided on the merits (28.4%–39.5%).
  3. That average hides large differences (Section 4): among the 22 agencies with at least 250 closed appeals in FY2021–25, from 2.8% to 59.4%; other closures make up 6.3% to 68.8% of the denominator. DOJ, large and low, pulls the average down.
  4. DHS is much higher, mainly at USCIS and CBP (Sections 2, 4 and 6): 48.2%–75.7% each year in FY2009–23. It fell to 39.0% and 36.7% in FY2024–25 because other closures rose from 17.8% to 43.3%; among appeals decided on the merits it did not fall (58.8%, 61.8%, 64.8%).
  5. DHS appeals surged (Section 5; one or two years of data): DHS received 6,050 appeals in FY2023 and 20,664 in FY2025, closed 12,707 in FY2025, and appeals pending at year end rose from 2,482 to 10,567. Two thirds of the added closures (4,412 of 6,583) were closures for other reasons, mainly at CBP, whose cited reasons are mostly procedural.
  6. Reversed or remanded does not mean records were released: the category includes remands for further processing.

What not to say:

  • Do not say "one third of denials are overturned": the base is closed appeals, and appeals received are fewer than 2 per 100 requests processed.
  • Do not rank agencies by reversal share: appeal arrangements differ, and other closures make up 6.3% to 68.8% of the denominator.
  • Do not say complete reversals doubled (13.4% to 25.7% government-wide): at DHS, partial reversals fell from 27.9% in FY2021 to 4.1% in FY2025 while complete reversals rose; outside DHS both are flat.
  • Do not read DHS's lower FY2024–25 share as stricter review: among appeals decided on the merits it did not fall.
  • Do not treat FY2008 as a normal year for DHS: USCIS closed 1,425 appeals for other reasons, citing two procedural reasons in Table 11.
  • Do not treat the FY2025 surge as settled: it is one year, and FY2025 has no following-year report to check against.
  • Do not read Table 10 reasons as the make-up of other closures: several may be cited per appeal, also for affirmed appeals.

Leads to follow up separately:

  • CBP's "no component response to adjudicate": 328 in FY2024, 1,155 in FY2025; worth reading alongside CBP's request backlog (Storyline 4, Section 8).
  • DHS cites "records not reasonably described" 742 times in FY2024 and "not agency record" 477 times in FY2025, far more than in other years.
  • DHS partial reversals fell from 27.9% to 4.1%.
  • Outside DHS, appeals per 100 processed fell from 1.92–2.37 to 1.55–1.78 from FY2023.

Methods and remaining questions¶

  • Reversed or remanded includes remands for further processing and does not mean the requester received records; the annual reports are not linked to final releases.
  • The two denominators answer different questions and are always labeled. Appeal arrangements differ across agencies (for example, in FY2025 only OIP reports appeals at DOJ), so these shares are not used to rank agencies.
  • Table 10 reasons may be cited several times per appeal and for affirmed appeals, so they are not a breakdown of Table 08 other closures; Table 11 is free text merged only by letter case, so its counts are lower bounds.
  • The Table 26 appeal-backlog column has 1,098 N/A entries, all at units that do not handle appeals separately; they count as zero in totals. The request-backlog column has none.
  • 26 agencies are missing in FY2008–09 (Section 2). FY2025 has no following-year report yet. The reports are self-reported; blank cells count as zero, and nothing is imputed.
  • Single-unit removal is descriptive; agencies without components count once (594 removals for all government, 572 outside DHS).

Data and reproduction¶

Source: data/component_master_no_03_06_11.csv. Table 07 appeals received, processed and pending at year end; Table 08 the four appeal outcomes; Table 10 non-exemption reasons cited on appeal; Table 01 requests processed (cross-checked with Table 02); Table 26 appeal backlog; Table 11 text from other_reasons_03_11.csv in the same folder. Shared functions are in storyline_lib.py; every figure quoted in the text is checked with an assertion.
